title: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (1 of 7)
hook: the first of three paths: what if the dishes were an offering?
tomorrow: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (2 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the silence after om, and the end of the Upanishads. Your line was the fourth: peaceful, auspicious, not two. Did you let one silence stay unfilled? Day two hundred sixty.

After four weeks in the depths of the Upanishads, a fair question: fine, but I have a job. I have kids, a commute, a sink full of dishes. When do I get to sit in the silence after om? The tradition's answer is a surprise. You don't have to leave the sink. Hindu teachers draw three great paths, three yogas, out of the Gita: karma, the path of action; bhakti, the path of devotion; and jnana, the path of knowledge. For the next three weeks we take them one at a time. And we start with the one that begins at the sink.
screen: `I HAVE A JOB.` → `THREE PATHS.` → `THE ONE THAT STARTS AT THE SINK.`

segments.voice: Karma, you learned on day seven, means action. Yoga means joining, yoking. Karma yoga is action that joins you to the divine, instead of tying you up in knots. How? The Gita's answer is worth holding up to the light. In chapter three, Krishna says the world is bound by action, except action done as yajna, as sacrifice, as offering. Work done as an offering doesn't bind. Then chapter nine makes it plain: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in worship, whatever you give, whatever discipline you keep, do it as an offering to me. Whatever you do. Not only the rituals. The eating counts. The giving counts. The spreadsheet counts. So an offering isn't a special kind of act. It's a way of holding any act. You do it as well as you can, and then you let it go, into the hands of God, or of the whole, the way you'd set a flower down at a shrine and walk away without taking it back. That's the move the Isha made at the start of the Upanishads, too: action that doesn't cling. Some Hindus say a word of offering before meals or before starting work, and some offer the fruits of the day at night. Over this week we'll also meet Swami Vivekananda, the Hindu monk who taught in America and gave a set of talks in New York later published as Karma-Yoga. He'll put it in his own blunt way. But the root is this: offer the work.
screen: `KARMA: ACTION. YOGA: JOINING.` · `ACTION AS SACRIFICE DOESN'T BIND.` · `WHATEVER YOU DO, AS AN OFFERING.` · `SET IT DOWN, AND WALK AWAY.` · then, large: `OFFER THE WORK.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Think of the next ordinary task on your list. Picture yourself doing it carefully, the way you'd prepare something for someone you love. Then picture finishing it and setting it down, the way you'd set down a flower, and walking away without looking back to see who noticed. If you pray, you can offer it silently to God as you understand God. If not, offer it to the people it will help, or to the day itself. The bell holds the time.
Karma yoga, action as offering. Whatever you do, eat, give or keep, done as an offering, doesn't bind.
Your line: offer the work. Today, pick one boring task and do it as an offering: carefully, then let it go. Day two hundred sixty.

howItsDone: A common Hindu practice is to offer food before eating and to dedicate work to God, drawing on Gita 9.27; some end the day by offering its actions and their results at the family shrine.

original.note: Sanskrit: karma yoga, the yoga of action; karma from kri, to do; yoga from yuj, to join.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma yoga means doing good deeds to earn good karma.
what it means: it's any action done as an offering, without clinging to the result.
what a scholar hears: Gita 3.9 (yajnarthat karmano 'nyatra loko 'yam karma-bandhanah) and 9.27 (yat karoshi yad ashnasi… tat kurushva mad-arpanam).

notes: Opens 'the three paths' (260–280); order karma, bhakti, jnana follows the outline.

'The monk who brought yoga to America in the 1890s' is a common simplification (Vivekananda, Parliament of Religions 1893); check phrasing. Karma-Yoga lectures given in New York, 1895–96; published 1896 — check.
Practices of offering before meals and dedicating work: widespread; check wording.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the three paths now framed as what Hindu teachers draw from the Gita (not something the Gita itself 'lays out'); cut 'one of the gentlest verses' and the listener-directed 'which you've read' / 'you know the answer already'; 'brought yoga to America in the 1890s' replaced with 'taught in America and gave talks in New York'; 'many Hindus still' softened; Isha timing corrected from 'three weeks ago'.
